title: Jansenius admits good works before justification, which the Protestants seem to deny
source_text: LIII. Verum est quidem Jansenium nihilominus statuere, cum Concilio Tridentino, opera quaedam bona ab homine fieri posse, priusquam sit justificatus, nec omnia opera quae fiunt ante justificationem esse peccata, & Deo displicere. Cujus contrarium Protestantes videntur communiter asserere, censura sua notantes Canonem Tridentinum, quo anathema dicitur quicunque dixerit, omnia opera quae fiunt ante justificationem, quacunque ratione facta sint, esse peccata.
pass_a_gloss: LIII. True it is indeed that Jansenius nevertheless lays down, with the Council of Trent, that certain good works can be done by man, before he be justified, nor that all works which are done before justification are sins, and displease God. The contrary of which the Protestants seem commonly to assert, marking with their censure the Tridentine Canon, by which anathema is said to whoever shall have said, that all works which are done before justification, in whatever manner they be done, are sins.
pass_b_english: Thesis LIII. It is true that Jansenius nonetheless holds, with the Council of Trent, that a man can do certain good works before he is justified, and that not all the works done before justification are sins and displeasing to God.

The Protestants seem commonly to assert the opposite when they censure the canon of Trent that pronounces anathema on anyone who says that all works done before justification, in whatever way they are done, are sins.

choices.why: Le Blanc's key distinction: justification strictly is the sinner's absolution for Christ's satisfaction; taken widely it includes the faith by which we are justified.
